hero.title: Photoelectric Effect — When Light Kicks Out Electrons
hero.hook: Why does a solar panel stop working if you shine radio waves on it, no matter how bright? The answer shook the foundations of classical physics — and it's a guaranteed 3-mark question in your boards.

hook_section.scenario: Cover a metal plate with UV light — electrons fly off instantly. Now switch to bright red light — no electrons at all, no matter how long you wait or how intense the beam. That's bizarre. More energy should mean more electrons. So why does colour matter more than brightness?
hook_section.bridge: Classical physics had no answer. Einstein did — and it won him the Nobel Prize. The photoelectric effect proved that light isn't just a wave. It comes in packets called photons, and each photon either has enough energy to kick an electron out, or it doesn't.
hook_section.punchline: Frequency decides if electrons leave. Intensity decides how many leave.

concept_section.analogy: Think of a bouncer at a club. Each photon is a person trying to get in. The bouncer has a minimum entry fee (the work function φ). If your photon can't pay the fee — no entry. Sending a crowd of underpaid photons (high intensity, low frequency) still gets nobody in. But one photon with enough energy gets through immediately.
concept_section.principle: Einstein's Photoelectric Equation: KE_max = hν − φ, where h = Planck's constant, ν = frequency of light, φ = work function of metal.
concept_section.reveal_prompt: Tap each factor to see its effect 👇

reveals.question: 🔵 What if frequency is below threshold?
reveals.answer: No photoelectric effect at all — regardless of intensity. The photon simply doesn't have enough energy to overcome the work function.

reveals.question: 🌊 What if I increase intensity (same frequency)?
reveals.answer: More photons hit the metal → more electrons are ejected → higher photocurrent. But KE_max of each electron stays the same.

reveals.question: ⬆️ What if frequency increases?
reveals.answer: Each photon has more energy → electrons leave with higher KE_max. Stopping potential increases.

reveals.question: ⚡ What is stopping potential?
reveals.answer: The reverse voltage needed to stop the most energetic electrons. eV₀ = KE_max = hν − φ. It depends only on frequency, not intensity.

points: Threshold frequency (ν₀): minimum frequency for emission; ν₀ = φ/h
Work function (φ): minimum energy to eject an electron from the metal surface
KE_max = hν − φ → increases with frequency, independent of intensity
Photocurrent increases with intensity (more photons → more electrons)
Emission is instantaneous — no time lag, confirms particle nature of light

exam_questions.question: Derive Einstein's photoelectric equation and explain stopping potential
Why does photoelectric effect not occur below threshold frequency?
How does stopping potential change when frequency of incident light is doubled?

quiz.q: In the photoelectric effect, increasing the intensity of incident light (above threshold frequency) will:
opts: Increase the KE of emitted electrons
Increase the number of emitted electrons
quiz.exp: Intensity means more photons per second. More photons eject more electrons → higher photocurrent. But each electron's energy depends only on frequency.

quiz.q: The stopping potential for a metal is 2V when light of frequency ν is used. If frequency is doubled, stopping potential becomes:
quiz.exp: eV₀ = hν − φ. Doubling ν doubles hν but φ stays constant, so the new V₀ = (2hν − φ)/e > 2×original V₀.

quiz.q: Which of the following proves the particle nature of light?
quiz.exp: Interference, diffraction and polarisation are wave phenomena. Photoelectric effect — where a single photon ejects one electron — proves light behaves as particles (photons).

quiz.q: The work function of a metal is 2 eV. The threshold frequency is: (h = 6.6×10⁻³⁴ J·s)

flipcards.back: Emission of electrons from a metal surface when light of sufficient frequency falls on it
Minimum energy needed to eject an electron from the metal surface; φ = hν₀
No effect — KE_max depends only on frequency, not intensity
Reverse voltage that stops the fastest electrons; eV₀ = hν − φ
